question:
Patient note:
A 63-year-old man with a fifteen-year history of alcohol-associated cirrhosis, last drink nine months ago after completion of an inpatient rehabilitation program, was rushed to the emergency assessment bay by emergency medical services at 06:40 because his partner found him unarousable except to painful stimulus, muttering incoherently, and picking at the bedclothes through the night; earlier that evening he had complained of vague malaise but still managed to watch television and eat half a sandwich before retiring. He has never required therapeutic paracentesis, has never been prescribed diuretics, and his prior outpatient ultrasounds consistently showed a shrunken nodular liver without intra-abdominal fluid. Previous complications were limited to two episodes of upper-gastrointestinal hemorrhage from small varices, the most recent three years ago, treated endoscopically with band ligation; he has been inconsistent with follow-up because of transportation barriers. Other medical problems include long-standing hypertension on lisinopril 10 mg daily, well-controlled type 2 diabetes managed with glipizide 5 mg twice daily, and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease related to a 40-pack-year smoking history—he quit five years ago. He takes no anticoagulants, herbal products, or vitamin K antagonists, and reports no medication allergies. Earlier yesterday he denied nausea, vomiting, abdominal distention, ankle swelling, pruritus, chest pain, dyspnea, fever, or chills. Family history is notable for a father who died of myocardial infarction at 70 and no relatives with liver disease. He lives in a single-story home, uses a cane because of hip osteoarthritis, and is independent in activities of daily living. On arrival to the bay—before any intravenous access, medication, or blood draw—vital signs were temperature 37.1 °C, blood pressure 102/60 mm Hg, heart rate 92 beats/min regular, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min with shallow excursions, and oxygen saturation 96 % on 2 L nasal cannula placed by paramedics en route. He lay supine with eyes half-open, emitted incomprehensible sounds, failed to follow commands, withdrew sluggishly to nail-bed pressure, and displayed a coarse irregular flap only when wrists were briefly extended by the examiner before drifting back to the mattress. Pupils were equal at 3 mm and reactive; corneal reflexes were intact, gag was present, tone was symmetrical though slightly decreased, and no focal deficits were elicited. Breath had a pungent sweet odor. Sclerae were deep yellow, and there were dozens of spider vascular lesions across the upper chest and shoulders. Mucous membranes were dry but without blood. Neck was supple; jugular venous pulsation approximated 7 cm H₂O at 30-degree elevation. Cardiac examination revealed a regular S1 and S2 without murmurs. Lung fields were clear to auscultation. The abdominal wall was flat with a sunken umbilicus, moved synchronously with respiration, remained tympanitic throughout on percussion, and exhibited no flank dullness or fluid wave even after an assistant stabilized the midline; palpation disclosed a firm, crenelated liver edge 2 cm below the right costal margin on gentle inspiration but no splenic tip. Bowel sounds were hypoactive yet present. There was no peripheral edema or muscle wasting beyond mild temporal hollowing. Point-of-care glucose measured 108 mg/dL. A focused bedside ultrasound performed immediately—still before blood samples, vitamin K, albumin, lactulose, rifaximin, diuretics, or antibiotics—confirmed a markedly heterogeneous liver with an indented capsule, patent portal vein with hepatopetal flow at 14 cm/s, spleen length 18 cm, and complete absence of anechoic fluid in Morison’s pouch, paracolic gutters, or pelvis; kidneys appeared normal in size and echogenicity, and the gallbladder was contracted without stones. Venous blood drawn via 20-gauge antecubital catheter ten minutes after arrival, prior to any therapy, returned total bilirubin 11.5 mg/dL, serum albumin 1.9 g/dL, alanine aminotransferase 71 U/L, aspartate aminotransferase 105 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 186 U/L, γ-glutamyl transferase 221 U/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, potassium 4.0 mmol/L, chloride 100 mmol/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L, blood urea nitrogen 24 mg/dL, creatinine 1.02 mg/dL (estimated GFR 78 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 12.2 g/dL, white blood cell count 7.8 ×10⁹/L, platelet count 86 ×10⁹/L, and a prothrombin time corresponding to an international normalized ratio of 3.25. Urinalysis obtained by straight catheterization showed 2+ bilirubin, moderate urobilinogen, no leukocyte esterase, and no nitrite. Upright chest radiography obtained immediately afterward revealed elevated diaphragms with clear lung fields, and a 12-lead electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus rhythm at 90 beats/min with a QTc of 438 ms. Up to the moment this note is written he has received no sedatives, no ammonia-lowering agents, no blood products, no vasopressors, and no intravenous fluids beyond the saline lock, ensuring that all clinical findings and laboratory values reflect his baseline physiologic state on presentation for profound alteration in mental status in the setting of advanced alcohol-related cirrhosis.

Question: What is the patient's Child-Pugh Score? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Child-Pugh score assigns 1–3 points to each of five criteria. Using the pretreatment admission findings:
- Total bilirubin: 11.5 mg/dL (>3) = 3 points.
- Albumin: 1.9 g/dL (<2.8) = 3 points.
- INR: 3.25 (>2.3) = 3 points.
- Ascites: absent on examination and ultrasound, without diuretic treatment = 1 point.
- Hepatic encephalopathy: incoherent and responsive only to painful stimulation, consistent with severe encephalopathy (grade III–IV scoring category) = 3 points.
Total = 3 + 3 + 3 + 1 + 3 = 13 (Child-Pugh class C).
Final answer: 13
